Adhesiolysis was performed through a lower midline laparotomy to allow an oncological, stapled, side-to-side, antiperistaltic SB resection. The SB lumen was significantly narrowed by the mass, and multiple enlarged, firm mesenteric lymph nodes were palpable. There was no evidence of metastatic disease.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 80-year-old man with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma on zanubrutinib presented to the ED with classic small bowel obstruction symptoms (colicky abdominal pain, obstipation, nausea, vomiting). An incidental non-obstructing small bowel mass had been identified 4 months prior during a febrile neutropenia admission. CT abdomen-pelvis on the current admission demonstrated a large obstructing distal small bowel mass that had increased in size compared to the prior study. Initial conservative management with nasogastric decompression, IV fluid resuscitation, and Gastrografin on day 2 achieved radiological resolution of the obstruction. However, the patient underwent surgical resection via laparotomy with adhesiolysis and stapled side-to-side antiperistaltic small bowel resection. Intraoperative findings included a mass adherent within the pelvis with significant luminal narrowing and multiple enlarged firm mesenteric lymph nodes; no metastatic disease was noted. Histopathology confirmed a 75 mm grade 2 jejunal leiomyosarcoma with negative margins and metastatic disease in 1 of 4 lymph nodes. The remaining three lymph nodes demonstrated features consistent with the patient's known lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. EBV-encoded RNA was negative, excluding EBV-associated leiomyosarcoma. The patient progressed well postoperatively and was discharged on postoperative day 7.
